claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles dispersed in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite has inherent interfacial defects that lead to phase separation and void formation.
W particles will be conformally precoated with an ultrathin WNx layer by ALD before composite consolidation.
ALD at 250–300 °C can produce a sub-nanometer to few-nanometer WNx coating on the W particles.
The coated composite is to be sintered at 800–900 °C under a reducing atmosphere.
The coating forms a nanoscale, uniform WNx interphase between W and Cu.
The WNx interphase improves wetting between W and Cu.
The WNx interphase improves bonding between W and Cu.
The WNx interphase lowers the interfacial-energy mismatch between W and Cu.
The WNx interphase acts as a barrier to W–Cu interdiffusion.
Improved wetting and inhibited interdiffusion suppress interfacial void nucleation and growth.
The WNx interphase inhibits phase separation during high-temperature treatment and irradiation.
The treated composite will have a more continuous and less defective W–Cu interface than an untreated composite.
The treated composite will contain fewer interfacial voids and exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite.
Reduced interfacial defects will improve the treated composite's thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite.
The interfacial and thermal-conductivity benefits will persist under cyclic high heat flux and neutron or proton irradiation relevant to W-based plasma-facing/Cu-based cooling joints.
Void formation and phase separation in untreated W–Cu composites degrade thermal conductivity.
The proposed service range is limited to temperatures below the degradation limit of the WNx interphase and irradiation fluxes typical of plasma-facing/cooling joints.
